pos: n. (one who declares another righteous; a title of God in the gospel)
etymology: From Latin justus, righteous, and facere, to make or declare — through Old French justifier. It renders the participle of Greek dikaioo, to pronounce righteous, a courtroom verb rather than a workshop one.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it is the hinge of Romans. Paul has spent two and a half chapters proving that every mouth is stopped and all the world guilty before God, and the question that follows is not how God can be merciful — anyone can be lenient — but how he can acquit the guilty without ceasing to be just. A judge who lets the wicked go is himself wicked; Proverbs says he that justifieth the wicked is abomination to the LORD. Paul's answer is the propitiation set forth in the blood of Christ, and the conclusion he draws is stated with deliberate care: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Not just although he justifies, and not merciful instead of just, but both at once, and by the same act. The cross is what makes the sentence lawful. Everything follows from that. God justifieth the ungodly, and the faith of the man who worketh not is counted for righteousness — counted, not created. It is God that justifieth, and therefore no charge can be laid against his elect. To call God the Justifier is to say that the verdict over a believing sinner is not a lowering of the standard but a satisfaction of it, obtained elsewhere and credited here.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who justifies; one who vindicates, defends or absolves; he that pardons and clears from guilt.
webster_full: JUSTIFIER, n. One who justifies; one who vindicates, supports or defends.
JUSTIFIER, n. He that pardons and absolves from guilt and punishment.
JUSTIFY, v.t. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment.
IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of; to reckon to one what does not belong to him.
PROPITIATION, n. The atonement or atoning sacrifice offered to God to assuage his wrath and render him propitious to sinners.
scriptures: Romans 3:26
To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
Romans 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Romans 8:33
Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth.
Galatians 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: Justification is softened into acceptance — God overlooking sin because he is loving — when Paul's whole labour is to show that God did not overlook it, and that the verdict cost a death.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular gospel says God accepts you as you are, and stops. Scripture says something more costly and more permanent. Acceptance without satisfaction would make God unjust, and an unjust God is no refuge for anyone — a judge who winks at one man's crimes will wink at the crimes committed against him. Paul insists that the mercy shewn to the believer was purchased at the price of the Son's blood, so that God is simultaneously the one who upholds the law and the one who acquits the lawbreaker. Remove the propitiation and justifier becomes a synonym for indulgence, and the comfort of Romans 8 evaporates with it: no charge can be laid only because the charge was already answered.

Rome's error runs the other way and is older: to make justification a process by which grace is infused and the sinner gradually made righteous enough to be declared so. The Confession answers that those whom God effectually calleth he also freely justifieth, not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous. The distinction is not academic. If the verdict waits on the process, no man knows where he stands; if the verdict is declared at once on the ground of Christ's obedience received by faith, then being justified by faith we have peace with God — present tense, and not subject to review.
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to declare righteous; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; logizomai (G3049), to reckon or impute; hilasterion (G2435), the propitiation.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to pronounce righteous; a forensic verb, used of a verdict and never of a repair.
Greek dikaion — just; Paul sets it beside justifier in one clause so that neither may be surrendered.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to place to an account; the accounting word of Romans 4.
Greek hilasterion (G2435) — the propitiation, the mercy seat; the ground on which the verdict is lawful.
Greek asebes (G765) — ungodly; the man God is said to justify, which is the offence and the gospel together.
usage: “that he might be just, and the justifier” — both held in one clause.
“him that justifieth the ungodly” — the only sort of man there is to justify.
“It is God that justifieth” — the answer to every accuser.

pos: n. (one who renders recompence; a title of God toward those who seek him)
etymology: From Old North French rewarder, to regard or take notice of — the same root as regard. To reward is first to look at, and only then to repay. It renders Greek misthapodotes, a payer of wages, used once in the New Testament.
biblical_def: Hebrews gives the shortest creed in Scripture and makes it the minimum for pleasing God: he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. Two articles only — that God exists, and that he repays the seeker. The second is not an afterthought. A man may grant that God is and still keep away, believing him indifferent, or capricious, or too great to notice; that man will not come. The Greek word is misthapodotes, a payer of wages, which sounds crude until one notices how freely Scripture uses the language of pay. Moses esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt, for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward — he did the arithmetic and found Egypt the poorer investment. The writer tells his readers not to cast away their confidence, which hath great recompence of reward. And the last chapter of the Bible has Christ saying my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be. None of this is wages earned; the same book grounds every blessing in a better covenant and a finished sacrifice. But the God who gives freely also repays deliberately, and the man who denies the second half is not more spiritual than Moses.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that rewards; one that recompenses or requites, whether for good or evil.
webster_full: REWARDER, n. One that rewards; one that recompenses or requites.
REWARD, n. Recompense, or equivalent return for good or evil done or received.
RECOMPENSE, n. An equivalent returned for anything given, done or suffered.
REQUITE, v.t. To repay; to recompense; to return an equivalent in good or evil.
DILIGENT, a. Steady in application to business; constant in effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
scriptures: Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Hebrews 10:35
Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward.
Hebrews 11:26
Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.
Revelation 22:12
And, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.
corruption_summary: Seeking reward from God is treated as mercenary and beneath mature faith; Hebrews makes it a required article of belief, while the prosperity trade corrupts it in the other direction by naming the reward ourselves.
corruption_paragraphs: A certain refined piety holds that a Christian should serve God for nothing, and that any eye to reward is selfishness. Hebrews will not allow it. The man who comes to God must believe that God rewards the seeker, and the chapter's heroes are commended precisely for reckoning on it: Abraham looked for a city, Moses had respect unto the recompence, and all of them died in faith having seen the promises afar off. To refuse the reward is not humility; it is a quiet accusation that God is not generous. The reward is himself — I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward — and a man who does not want that has not begun to seek.

The opposite corruption is louder and does more visible damage. The prosperity teacher agrees that God rewards, and then specifies the currency: health, money, promotion, the car in the driveway. Hebrews 11 answers by listing what the rewarded actually received — mockings and scourgings, bonds and imprisonment, stoned, sawn asunder, wandering in deserts and mountains, of whom the world was not worthy — and then says these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise. God is a rewarder. He has never once agreed to let the seeker name the reward or the date.
roots_summary: Greek misthapodotes (G3406), a payer of wages; misthos (G3408), wages or reward; ekzeteo (G1567), to seek out diligently; Hebrew sakar (H7939), hire or reward.
roots_lines: Greek misthapodotes (G3406) — one who pays wages; used only of God, and only here.
Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, hire, reward; the workman is worthy of it, and so is the prophet received in a prophet's name.
Greek ekzeteo (G1567) — to seek out, to search for earnestly; the diligence is in the verb, not added by the translators.
Greek misthapodosia (G3405) — the recompence of reward; the noun Moses reckoned with.
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — wages, reward; I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward to Abram.
usage: “he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” — an article of the minimum creed.
“he had respect unto the recompence of the reward” — Moses doing the arithmetic.
“my reward is with me” — the reward carried by the rewarder himself.

pos: n. (one that distinguishes or judges; a title given to the word of God)
etymology: From Latin discernere, to separate or distinguish — dis-, apart, and cernere, to sift or separate. It renders Greek kritikos, able to judge, from which we have critic: the word of God is the critic, and the reader is the text.
biblical_def: Hebrews calls the word of God quick and powerful, sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. The Greek is kritikos. Scripture is the critic; we are not its reviewers. The image is surgical and uncomfortable: a blade that goes past where any human blade stops, through the seam where soul and spirit are joined, into the marrow of a man's motives, and distinguishes his thoughts from his intents — what he considered from what he actually meant. The next verse drops the figure and names the surgeon: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do. Discernment therefore runs one direction before it runs the other. A man cannot judge the word, because the word is already judging him; and he cannot judge himself accurately, because the heart is deceitful above all things — it is the LORD who searches it. Only after that does Scripture ask believers to discern: to try the spirits, to prove all things, to have senses exercised to discern both good and evil. That discernment is a trained faculty, and it is trained by the blade.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that discerns, distinguishes, perceives or judges; one who sees or discriminates with accuracy.
webster_full: DISCERNER, n. One that discerns, distinguishes, perceives or judges.
DISCERN, v.t. To separate by the eye or by the understanding; to distinguish; to make a difference between.
DISCERNMENT, n. The power or faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes one thing from another; acuteness of judgment.
INTENT, n. Design; purpose; drift; aim; that which is intended.
MARROW, n. A soft, oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones; the inner and best part.
scriptures: Hebrews 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Hebrews 4:13
Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
1 Corinthians 2:14
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Jeremiah 17:10
I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.
corruption_summary: Discernment is reduced to personal intuition — a feeling about a teacher or a book — while Scripture makes the word itself the discerner and the believer the one discerned before he discerns anything.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite failures share one root. The first calls suspicion discernment: a hard eye, a ready verdict, a ministry of detecting error in others that never turns the blade inward. Hebrews orders the operation the other way. The sword is in God's hand, the marrow being divided is mine, and the first fruit of real discernment is a man who has been found out. The second failure calls impression discernment: I sensed something, I had a check in my spirit, offered as evidence and treated as unanswerable. John gives an objective test instead — try the spirits whether they are of God, and the test is a confession about Christ come in the flesh, not a feeling in the room.

Paul adds the limit that keeps discernment humble. The natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God, because they are spiritually discerned — the faculty is not native to fallen men and cannot be acquired by education or sharpened by cynicism. It is given with the Spirit and exercised by use: strong meat belongs to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil. So discernment grows the way a palate grows, on a steady diet of the word that is doing the discerning.
roots_summary: Greek kritikos (G2924), able to judge or discern; enthumesis (G1761), a thought or deliberation; ennoia (G1771), intent or purpose; anakrino (G350), to examine or discern.
roots_lines: Greek kritikos (G2924) — skilled in judging; used once, and of the word of God rather than of a man.
Greek enthumesis (G1761) — what a man turns over in his mind; rendered thoughts.
Greek ennoia (G1771) — the settled intention behind the thought; rendered intents.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to sift, to examine judicially; he that is spiritual judgeth all things.
Greek trachelizo (G5136) — to lay bare the neck; the vivid verb behind opened in the next verse.
usage: “a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” — the word as critic.
“all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him” — the figure dropped, the person named.
“because they are spiritually discerned” — the faculty is not natural.

pos: n. (one who keeps from harm or destruction; a title of God spoken by Job)
etymology: From Latin praeservare, to guard beforehand — prae-, before, and servare, to keep or watch. In Job it renders a participle of Hebrew natsar, to watch, guard, keep.
biblical_def: Job says it from the bottom of his affliction, and that is what gives the title its weight: I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? He is not paying a compliment. He is confessing that the God who has made him a target is the same God who keeps men alive, and he cannot get away from either fact. That is the honest position of a sufferer who has not let go of doctrine. Elsewhere the preserving is stated flatly and warmly: The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul; he preserveth the souls of his saints and delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked. Nehemiah's prayer widens it to everything that exists — thou hast made heaven and earth and the seas and all that is therein, and thou preservest them all. So preservation is a doctrine of two ranges. God upholds all things by the word of his power, so that no creature holds itself in being for a moment; and God keeps his own people, so that none is lost. Job had lost nearly everything and still addressed him by the title. That is the point of the book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who preserves; one who saves or defends from destruction or evil; that which preserves.
webster_full: PRESERVER, n. One who preserves; one who saves or defends from destruction or evil.
PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil.
PRESERVATION, n. The act of preserving or keeping safe; the act of keeping from injury, destruction or decay.
UPHOLD, v.t. To lift on high; to elevate; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling.
MARK, n. A visible line made by drawing one substance on another; a butt; anything to be aimed at.
scriptures: Job 7:20
I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself?
Psalm 121:7
The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.
Psalm 97:10
Ye that love the LORD, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked.
Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
corruption_summary: Preservation is read as a promise of comfortable circumstances; Job speaks the title while covered in boils, and the Psalm that promises it is sung by pilgrims walking exposed roads.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's preserving of his people is not a guarantee of their circumstances. Psalm 121 is a song of degrees, sung by men on the road to Jerusalem where the hills held robbers, and it does not promise an easy journey — it promises a keeper who does not sleep. The same God who preserves the soul let Job lose his children, and let Stephen be stoned, and let the apostles be beaten, and never once broke the promise. What is preserved is the soul, and the preserving is proved not by the absence of the arrow but by the survival of the man.

The doctrine has a second range that steadies the first. Nehemiah's prayer says God made heaven and earth and preservest them all, and Hebrews says the Son upholds all things by the word of his power. Creation is not a machine wound up and left running; it continues because it is continually held. Once that is seen, the personal promise stops sounding sentimental. The arm that keeps the stars in their courses is the arm underneath a believer, and Job, who could not understand what was happening to him, still knew whose arm it was.
roots_summary: Hebrew natsar (H5341), to watch, guard, keep; shamar (H8104), to keep or preserve; chayah (H2421), to keep alive; Greek phero (G5342), to bear or uphold.
roots_lines: Hebrew natsar (H5341) — to watch over, to guard; the participle Job addresses as preserver of men.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep; the repeated verb of Psalm 121, six times in eight verses.
Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to preserve alive; used of Joseph in Egypt, sent before his brethren to save life.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, uphold; the Son upholding all things by the word of his power.
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, to guard; Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me.
usage: “O thou preserver of men” — spoken by a man on an ash heap.
“he shall preserve thy soul” — the promise stated without qualification.
“he preserveth the souls of his saints” — the keeping that outlasts the circumstance.

pos: n. (one who restores what is broken down; a name promised to a people who fast rightly)
etymology: From Latin reparare, to make ready again — re-, again, and parare, to prepare. In Isaiah it renders a participle of Hebrew gadar, to wall up or close a breach, the same root behind the man sought to stand in the gap.
biblical_def: Isaiah 58 is a rebuke of religious performance. Israel fasted and bowed the head like a bulrush and complained that God had not noticed; God answers that the fast he has chosen is to loose the bands of wickedness, undo the heavy burdens, let the oppressed go free, deal bread to the hungry and bring the poor that are cast out into the house. Then comes the promise, and it is a promise of a name: thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in. A breach is a gap in a city wall — the place where defence has failed and an enemy walks in. To repair it is unglamorous, heavy, outdoor work, done in the open where the damage is visible. The reward for a true fast is not a feeling but a reputation for mending what other people broke. Nehemiah did exactly this, and his account records that the people had a mind to work, which is the whole secret. Amos sees God himself taking up the trade: I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof. And Isaiah 61 promises that the people so restored shall build the old wastes and repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations. Mended men mend.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who repairs; one who mends or restores to a sound state; one who makes amends.
webster_full: REPAIRER, n. One who repairs; one who restores to a sound state; one who makes amends.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation or partial destruction.
BREACH, n. The act of breaking; a gap in a wall, or in any solid body; a rupture.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former good state; to repair; to bring back to its former state.
DESOLATION, n. Destruction; a laying waste; a place deserted or laid waste.
scriptures: Isaiah 58:12

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
Nehemiah 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
Amos 9:11
In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:
Isaiah 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 58 is quoted as a proof text for social programmes detached from repentance, or else avoided entirely by churches that hear justice language and assume the world is speaking; the chapter is God rebuking his own people for a hollow fast.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is regularly enlisted for causes it never names, as though God were commissioning a political movement and the fast were a fundraiser. What God actually addresses is a congregation that kept the forms of worship while behaving like everyone else the other six days: fasting for strife and debate, exacting labour, hiding from their own flesh. The repair in view begins at home — bread to the hungry, the poor brought into the house, the naked covered — and it is commanded to a people who are told in the same chapter to call the sabbath a delight and honour God by not doing their own ways. Strip out the repentance and the sabbath and what is left is not Isaiah 58.

The reaction against that abuse has produced its own loss. Because justice language has been captured, sound churches have grown shy of the very words God uses, and the result is congregations that would rather debate the abuse than loose one heavy burden. Isaiah gives the name to those who do the work: repairer of the breach, restorer of paths to dwell in. It is a builder's name, earned outdoors, in the gap, where the wall is down. James says pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world — both halves, and neither one a substitute for the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadar (H1443), to wall up or close a breach; perets (H6556), a breach or gap; shuv (H7725), to restore or turn back; chorbah (H2723), a waste place.
roots_lines: Hebrew gadar (H1443) — to wall up, to hedge; the participle rendered repairer.
Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach; the gap in the wall, and the name of Judah's son Pharez.
Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to turn back, to restore; behind the restorer of paths to dwell in.
Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a desolation, a waste; what the repairers are sent to rebuild.
Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth or tabernacle; the fallen tabernacle of David that God himself repairs.
usage: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach” — a name given for a true fast.
“for the people had a mind to work” — Nehemiah's whole secret.
“close up the breaches thereof” — God taking up the trade himself.

pos: n. (one who raises up; in the Psalm, a title of the LORD toward a hunted man)
etymology: From Old Norse lypta, to raise, from a root meaning air or sky — to lift is to move a thing toward the sky. In Psalm 3 it renders a participle of Hebrew rum, to be high, to raise.
biblical_def: The title is given in the worst circumstance David ever wrote from. The superscription of Psalm 3 places it when he fled from Absalom his son: his own child leading the rebellion, the kingdom gone, the people multiplied that rise up against him, and many saying of his soul, there is no help for him in God. Against all of that David says three things about the LORD in one breath — thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head. A shield for the danger, glory for the shame, and a lifting for the head that shame had bowed. The picture is exact: a man walking out of his own city in disgrace, weeping, with his head covered, and the only hand under his chin is God's. What follows in the psalm is not deliverance but sleep — I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me — which is its own kind of proof. The rest of Scripture makes the lifting a settled way of God: he raiseth up all those that be bowed down; humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up. The order never reverses. The bowing is ours; the lifting is his.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that lifts or raises; that which raises or elevates.
webster_full: LIFTER, n. One that lifts or raises.
LIFT, v.t. To raise; to elevate; to bear or carry upward.
LIFT, v.t. To exalt; to elevate in rank, condition or estimation.
SHIELD, n. A broad piece of defensive armor; a buckler; used in war for the defense of the body.
BOW, v.i. To bend; to stoop; to bend the body in token of respect or submission.
scriptures: Psalm 3:3
But thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.
Psalm 27:6
And now shall mine head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me: therefore will I offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy; I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto the LORD.
James 4:10
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.
Psalm 145:14
The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that be bowed down.
corruption_summary: Self-esteem is offered as the cure for a bowed head, which puts the lifting in the sufferer's own hands; the Psalm gives the hand to God and reaches David at the moment when he had nothing left to esteem.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic answer to a man in David's condition is to raise his own estimate of himself — to talk to himself about his worth until his head comes up. Psalm 3 does something else entirely. David does talk to himself, but what he says is not about David: thou, O LORD, art a shield for me. The head comes up because of who is holding it, not because the man has been persuaded he deserves better. This matters because self-esteem fails exactly where David was — in a case where the accusations are partly true. He had sinned in the matter of Uriah, and Absalom's rebellion stood in the long shadow of it. A man in that position cannot lift his own head honestly. Someone else has to.

There is a churchly version of the same error, which tells the downcast to have more faith, as though the lifting were a technique to be mastered. James puts the sequence the other way: humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up — the promise attaches to the man who goes lower, not to the man who tries harder. God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble. So the counsel to the bowed head is not to think better of itself but to bow further, into the hands of the one who raiseth up all those that be bowed down, and then to sleep as David did while the trouble was still outside the door.
roots_summary: Hebrew rum (H7311), to be high, to raise up; rosh (H7218), the head; magen (H4043), a shield; kavod (H3519), glory or weight.
roots_lines: Hebrew rum (H7311) — to lift, to exalt; the participle behind the lifter up of mine head.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — the head; covered in mourning, lifted in restoration.
Hebrew magen (H4043) — a shield; the first of the three titles David stacks in one verse.
Hebrew kavod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; what a disgraced king had lost and God still was to him.
Greek hupsoo (G5312) — to lift up, to exalt; he shall lift you up in James, and the Son of man lifted up in John.
usage: “my glory, and the lifter up of mine head” — three titles in one breath, in flight.
“he shall lift you up” — the promise attached to going lower.
“raiseth up all those that be bowed down” — the settled habit of God.

pos: n. (one who cures or binds up; in Isaiah, an office a man refuses to take)
etymology: Old English haelan, to make whole — the same root as whole, hale and holy. To heal is to make entire. In Isaiah 3 it renders Hebrew chabash, to bind up, as a bandage binds a wound.
biblical_def: The word appears in a strange place. Isaiah is describing the collapse of Judah, when the state is so broken that men will grab a brother in the street and say, thou hast clothing, be thou our ruler — and the brother will swear in that day, I will not be an healer; for in my house is neither bread nor clothing: make me not a ruler of the people. The Hebrew is chabash, to bandage. To rule, in Isaiah's vocabulary, is to bind up wounds; and the mark of a society under judgment is that no one will take the bandage. Against that refusal Scripture sets the LORD who does not refuse. I am the LORD that healeth thee is given at Marah, where bitter water was made sweet by a tree cast into it, and it is given as a name. He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds — the same binding verb, now in God's hands, and applied to an injury no physician can reach. Christ took the title as his own work when he quoted the proverb Physician, heal thyself back to Nazareth, and he had opened his ministry there by reading Isaiah's commission to bind up the brokenhearted. The men of Isaiah 3 would not be healers. The Son of God came to be one, and was wounded doing it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that cures or heals; that which makes whole or restores to soundness.
webster_full: HEALER, n. One that cures or heals.
HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound and restore to soundness; to make whole.
HEAL, v.t. To reconcile, as a breach or difference; to make whole; to free from evil.
BIND, v.t. To tie together, or confine with a cord or bandage.
PHYSICIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases.
scriptures: Isaiah 3:7
In that day shall he swear, saying, I will not be an healer; for in my house is neither bread nor clothing: make me not a ruler of the people.
Exodus 15:26

And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.
Psalm 147:3
He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
Luke 4:23
And he said unto them, Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country.
corruption_summary: Healing is claimed as a right the believer may command and marketed by men who bill for it; Scripture presents it as the free act of a sovereign physician who sometimes says, my grace is sufficient for thee.
corruption_paragraphs: The faith-healing trade takes a real promise and turns it into a contract: God has already purchased your healing, so claim it, and if nothing happens the failure is yours. The pastoral cruelty of this is hard to overstate — it lays the weight of an unhealed body on the sick person's faith. Scripture refuses the arrangement outright. Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick. Timothy was told to take a little wine for his stomach's sake and his often infirmities. Paul himself besought the Lord thrice about the thorn and was answered not with healing but with my grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. No apostle ever told a sick believer that his sickness was evidence against him.

The opposite error quietly stops asking. Because the abuse is so visible, sober churches can drift into a practical cessationism of prayer — not denying that God heals, simply never expecting it. James gives plain instruction against that drift: is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. The God who is named the LORD that healeth thee has not retired. He heals whom he will, when he will, and finally and completely on a morning when there shall be no more pain, for the former things are passed away.
roots_summary: Hebrew rapha (H7495), to heal or mend; chabash (H2280), to bind up as with a bandage; Greek iaomai (G2390), to cure; iatros (G2395), a physician.
roots_lines: Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to repair; behind the covenant name Jehovah-rophe, the LORD that healeth thee.
Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up, to bandage; rendered healer in Isaiah 3 and bindeth up in Psalm 147.
Greek iaomai (G2390) — to cure, to heal; used of bodies and of souls, by whose stripes ye were healed.
Greek therapeuo (G2323) — to attend, to treat, to heal; the root behind therapy.
Greek iatros (G2395) — a physician; they that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
usage: “I will not be an healer” — the office refused in a collapsing nation.
“I am the LORD that healeth thee” — given at Marah as a name.
“He healeth the broken in heart” — an injury beyond any physician.

pos: n. (one who cleanses by removing what is foreign; a title of the coming Lord in Malachi)
etymology: From Latin purus, clean, and facere, to make. In Malachi it renders a participle of Hebrew taher, to be clean, used of metal cleared of its alloy and of a man cleared of defilement — the same word in both.
biblical_def: Malachi answers the people who had been saying, where is the God of judgment? He tells them the Lord they seek shall suddenly come to his temple — and then asks who may abide the day of his coming, for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap. Two trades, both violent in their way: the smelter who melts metal until the dross rises, and the fuller who beats and scours cloth with harsh lye. Then: he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness. Notice where he starts. Not with the pagan nations, nor even with the unfaithful laity, but with the priesthood — judgment begins at the house of God. And notice the verb: he shall sit. The refiner does not light the fire and leave; he sits by the crucible, watching, because silver over-fired is ruined and under-fired is still impure. The purpose is stated and it is not punishment: that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness. The fire exists to make worship acceptable. Titus says the same of Christ's death — he gave himself to purify unto himself a peculiar people — and John says every man that hath this hope purifieth himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which purifies or cleanses; one who purifies or makes clean; one who frees from mixture.
webster_full: PURIFIER, n. That which purifies or cleanses; a cleanser; a refiner.
PURIFY, v.t. To make pure or clear from extraneous admixture; to free from pollution.
REFINE, v.t. To purify; to clear from dross or recrement; to separate from extraneous matter.
DROSS, n. The recrement or despumation of metals; the scum of metals thrown off in melting.
FULLER, n. One whose occupation is to full and cleanse cloth.
scriptures: Malachi 3:3
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.
Malachi 3:2
But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:
Titus 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
1 John 3:3
And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure.
corruption_summary: Purity is reframed as authenticity — being unmixed about who you already are — while Malachi's purifier removes what is genuinely in the metal and does it with fire the metal did not choose.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary counterfeit of purity is authenticity. Be true to yourself, unmixed, unmasked. It sounds adjacent to holiness and is its opposite: authenticity asks a man to express what is in him, and purification exists because what is in him is the problem. The refiner's fire does not help silver be more itself; it burns off what has been in the ore since it came out of the ground. Nor is the process chosen by the silver. The Lord comes suddenly to his temple, and the question Malachi asks — who may abide the day of his coming? — assumes that no one would volunteer for this.

There is a churchly distortion too, in which purity is reduced to a list of things not done, usually things visible to other people. Malachi aims at the priests, who kept the list professionally and offered polluted bread on the altar while saying, wherein have we polluted thee? The purifying he describes reaches motives, and its end is not a cleaner record but an acceptable offering. John gives the believer his part: every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure — an active work, grounded in a hope and measured by a Person, not by the congregation next door.
roots_summary: Hebrew taher (H2891), to be clean or pure; tsaraph (H6884), to smelt or refine; zaqaq (H2212), to strain or purge; Greek katharizo (G2511), to cleanse.
roots_lines: Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean; the participle rendered purifier, used of metal and of men alike.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to smelt, to refine, to test; the refiner who sits by the crucible.
Hebrew borith (H1287) — lye or soap; the fuller's harsh alkali, the second figure in the pair.
Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse; the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
Greek hagnizo (G48) — to purify oneself; the verb John uses of the believer's own work.
usage: “he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver” — the refiner does not leave the fire.
“that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness” — the purpose of the burning.
“purify unto himself a peculiar people” — the purchase and the cleansing in one act.

pos: n. (one who runs to help another in distress; Paul's word for Phebe)
etymology: From Latin succurrere, to run beneath or run to help — sub-, under, and currere, to run. The help is not sent from a distance; the succourer goes under the load. It renders Greek prostatis, a patroness or one who stands before another.
biblical_def: Paul closes Romans by commending Phebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, and asks the Romans to receive her and assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of, for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also. The Greek prostatis means one who stands before another to help — a patroness, a protector, one who puts her own standing and resources between a needy person and their need. Paul, who could say he had learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content, says plainly that this woman had helped him. The Latin behind our English word says it even better: to succour is to run underneath, to get beneath a weight someone else is failing to carry. That is why the word belongs supremely to Christ: in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted. He is qualified to run underneath our load because he has carried it. And God speaks of himself the same way through Isaiah, quoted by Paul: in the day of salvation have I succoured thee. The order runs from God to the church and out through people like Phebe — helped, so helping; run to, so running.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that affords relief; a helper; one that runs to the aid of another in difficulty or distress.
webster_full: SUCCOURER, n. He that affords relief; a helper; a deliverer.
SUCCOUR, v.t. To run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress.
RELIEVE, v.t. To free, wholly or partially, from pain, grief, want, anxiety or distress.
PATRONESS, n. A female that favors or supports; a woman that protects or countenances.
ASSIST, v.t. To help; to aid; to succor; to give support to in some undertaking.
scriptures: Romans 16:2
That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also.
Hebrews 2:18
For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.
2 Corinthians 6:2
(For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)
Psalm 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
corruption_summary: Phebe is enlisted as a proof text in the argument over the pastoral office, which loses the woman entirely; Paul commends her for what she did — she stood between many believers and their need, including him.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 16:1-2 has been fought over so long that Phebe herself has nearly disappeared behind the argument. One side presses diakonos and prostatis into an office of rule; the other, wary of the move, hurries past her in two sentences. Both lose what Paul actually wrote. He names her, commends her to a church that had never met her, asks that she be received in the Lord as becometh saints, asks that they assist her in whatsoever business she has, and gives the reason: she has been a succourer of many, and of Paul. That is a substantial, costly, publicly acknowledged ministry, and the apostle who elsewhere orders the offices of the church is the one honouring it.

The honest reading holds both. Scripture reserves the office of elder to qualified men, and Scripture fills its pages with women whose labour the church could not have done without — the women who ministered to Christ of their substance, Priscilla who expounded the way of God more perfectly to Apollos, Lydia whose house received the first church in Europe, Phebe carrying a letter to Rome. A church that uses the New Testament's order as a reason to leave such women unnamed and unassisted has not obeyed the New Testament. Paul's instruction about Phebe is a command with a practical object: receive her, and help her.
roots_summary: Greek prostatis (G4368), a patroness, one who stands before; boetheo (G997), to run to the aid of a cry; diakonos (G1249), a servant; Hebrew azar (H5826), to help.
roots_lines: Greek prostatis (G4368) — one who stands before another as protector; used once, of Phebe.
Greek boetheo (G997) — to run at a cry for help; the verb rendered succour in Hebrews 2 and in the Syrophenician's Lord, help me.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant or minister; Paul's word for Phebe's relation to the church at Cenchrea.
Hebrew azar (H5826) — to help, to surround with aid; the root of Ebenezer, the stone of help.
Latin succurrere — to run underneath; the picture our English word preserves better than the Greek.
usage: “she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also” — an apostle admitting he was helped.
“he is able to succour them that are tempted” — qualified by having carried it.
“in the day of salvation have I succoured thee” — God running underneath first.

pos: n. (one who reproves sharply; a title God claims toward a nation that would not hear)
etymology: From Old North French rebuker, to beat back — re-, back, and buchier, to strike or fell timber. A rebuke is a blow that stops a man rather than one that destroys him. In Hosea it renders Hebrew musar, chastening instruction.
biblical_def: Hosea 5 is addressed to priests, to the house of Israel and to the house of the king, and the charge is that they have been a snare and a net to the people. In the middle of it God says something almost wistful: the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all. They were deep in their wickedness — profound, the word suggests going down into it — and the whole time God had been rebuking. The title is therefore an act of mercy that was refused. Rebuke in Scripture is never contempt; it is a blow struck to stop a man walking off a cliff. The risen Christ says it to a church he is about to spit out of his mouth: As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent. The rebuke is evidence of the love, not an interruption of it. Proverbs marks the dividing line between the two kinds of men: reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee; rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee. And Paul lays the duty on the ministry — reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and doctrine — joining the sharpness to patience and to teaching, so that it may never be mistaken for temper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that rebukes; a chider; one that reprehends or reproves with sharpness.
webster_full: REBUKER, n. One that rebukes; a chider; one that reprehends.
REBUKE, v.t. To chide; to reprove; to reprehend for a fault; to check by reproof.
REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure; to charge with a fault to the face.
CHASTEN, v.t. To correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender.
LONGSUFFERING, n. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.
scriptures: Hosea 5:2
And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all.
Revelation 3:19
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
Proverbs 9:8
Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
2 Timothy 4:2
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Rebuke is treated as incompatible with love, so it is either abolished as harmful or performed without the longsuffering and doctrine Paul binds to it; Christ says he rebukes the ones he loves.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of the age is that to correct someone is to harm them, and that acceptance is the only recognised form of love. Under that rule the pulpit goes quiet, church discipline lapses, and friends watch each other walk into ruin while congratulating themselves on being non-judgmental. Christ, writing to Laodicea, says the opposite in seven words: as many as I love, I rebuke and chasten. The letter is the sharpest in Revelation and it is addressed to people he calls beloved. A church that has abolished rebuke has not become more loving; it has quietly decided that nothing anyone does matters enough to mention.

The corrective has its own abuse. Paul does not say rebuke and stop; he says reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine — three verbs bound to two conditions. Longsuffering means the rebuker has borne with the man a long while and is not relieving his own irritation. Doctrine means the rebuke is from Scripture and not from taste. Where either is missing, what results is temper wearing the clothes of faithfulness, and Proverbs warns it will accomplish nothing anyway: the scorner will hate you, and only the wise man will love you for it. God himself was a rebuker of Israel for generations before the judgment fell.
roots_summary: Hebrew musar (H4148), chastening instruction; yakach (H3198), to reprove or argue a case; Greek elegcho (G1651), to convict or expose; epitimao (G2008), to rebuke sharply.
roots_lines: Hebrew musar (H4148) — discipline, chastening, instruction; behind a rebuker of them all.
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, to argue, to decide a case; rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, to expose to the light; rendered reprove, and used of the Spirit convicting the world.
Greek epitimao (G2008) — to censure sharply; used of Christ rebuking fevers, winds and devils.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train a child by discipline; the chasten paired with rebuke in Revelation 3.
usage: “I have been a rebuker of them all” — mercy offered and refused for generations.
“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten” — the rebuke as evidence of the love.
“with all longsuffering and doctrine” — the two conditions on the duty.
